claims.text: Superconductivity in high-entropy alloys is predominantly governed by electron–phonon coupling.
Configurational disorder modulates the strength of electron–phonon coupling.
Rapid quenching induces greater atomic disorder than slow cooling.
Increased atomic disorder alters the phonon spectrum.
The disorder-induced alteration of the phonon spectrum reduces effective electron–phonon coupling.
Reduced effective electron–phonon coupling lowers the superconducting transition temperature.
High-temperature annealing followed by slow cooling promotes a relatively ordered atomic configuration.
Rapid quenching freezes in a relatively disordered atomic configuration.
Local atomic disorder changes the phonon modes available for Cooper pairing.
Slow cooling produces a phonon spectrum more favorable for electron–phonon coupling than rapid quenching.
Rapidly quenched samples will have a lower superconducting transition temperature than slowly cooled samples.
The two thermal treatments will produce measurable phonon-spectrum differences correlated with disorder.
Secondary phases, magnetic impurities, or segregated regions can introduce additional superconducting pair-breaking mechanisms.
The magnitude and direction of the disorder-induced change in transition temperature can depend on alloy composition and the extent of disorder.
Failure of the higher-disorder quenched samples to exhibit a lower transition temperature would falsify the stated directional hypothesis.
Absence of phonon-spectrum differences correlated with transition-temperature variation would falsify the proposed phonon-mediated mechanism.
